<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-adadsf-0ee93157" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cffc38b1cb7d9602">Why not give each AdaDSF layer the same token budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Layers transform inputs by different amounts. Dense-teacher similarities allocate more to stronger transformations; routers and sparse paths then align with the teacher.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A nearly identity layer may need fewer active tokens than one that reorganizes features.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cffc38b1cb7d9602">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adadsf" data-paper-title="Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-641401c9edeae52a">Why give more compute to AdaDSF layers with lower input/output similarity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Lower cosine suggests a stronger representation transformation. Dense calibration maps layer differences to a globally corrected budget. Layer routers choose tokens and others bypass residually; allocation and alignment training serve different roles.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With fixed total budget, run the more transformative layer on more tokens instead of uniformly skipping half in each.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-641401c9edeae52a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adadsf" data-paper-title="Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a31595da2cce6b4">What controls should AdaDSF share with Uniform Mixture-of-Depths?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Match global budget, teacher initialization, alignment steps, and optimizer. Vary layerwise allocation. The local negative result shows adaptation is not necessarily better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Comparing 80% and 50% retention confounds strategy with compute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a31595da2cce6b4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:adadsf" data-paper-title="Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-25065d84348e3527">Should tokens outside layer top-k be removed?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aadadsf">Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei ACS Lab / Southern University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Bypass the block with the residual and merge in original order. Correct layer ratios to the global budget. Dropping/reordering positions changes later attention and teacher alignment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Token five can skip one layer but stays at position five for the next.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21291">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21291-adadsf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-25065d84348e3527">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:blt" data-paper-title="Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-blt-d95f5fc6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ba183b837163027f">Why put patches between bytes and global attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ablt">Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta FAIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Per-byte global compute is costly. Next-byte uncertainty forms variable patches and local encoders/decoders bridge them to byte inputs and outputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Predictable bytes can group more densely than difficult spans.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09871">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2412.09871-blt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ba183b837163027f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:blt" data-paper-title="Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d5226d54fcb95718">Why doesn&#x27;t BLT pay equal global compute for every byte?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ablt">Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta FAIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Local modules handle bytes, entropy sets variable patch boundaries, and global attention operates on patches before local byte decoding. Easy spans can use longer patches. This saves global interactions, not byte handling, and is not fixed tokenization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated patterns can produce fewer global patches than equally long unpredictable bytes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09871">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2412.09871-blt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d5226d54fcb95718">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:blt" data-paper-title="Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-78f525e2821c69ee">How do BLT boundaries differ from fixed tokenizer boundaries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ablt">Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta FAIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed tokenizer uses predefined subword rules. BLT uses prefix-dependent next-byte entropy, changing compute granularity by uncertainty.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same character sequence may get different boundaries in different contexts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09871">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2412.09871-blt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-78f525e2821c69ee">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:blt" data-paper-title="Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a1616b71881dbc14">Why isn&#x27;t the local surprisal boundary path full BLT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ablt">Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta FAIR</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A 512-symbol tokenizer approximates bytes with learned boundaries and shared latents, but does not implement full local encoders/decoders or 8B training. Do not label the approximate alphabet raw bytes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Boundary-aware grouping alone does not supply the complete byte-to-byte architecture.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09871">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2412.09871-blt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a1616b71881dbc14">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ce-guided-moe" data-paper-title="Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-ce-guided-moe-5d9cde32" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1df0094107045dd3">What do affinity and token error express?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ace-guided-moe">Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Bar-Ilan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Affinity is original router preference, while predicted error estimates quality for this token. Correct logits before top-k and supervise the head with actual next-token CE.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A strongly matched expert can still be bad at that token type.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37751">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37751-ce-guided-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1df0094107045dd3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ce-guided-moe" data-paper-title="Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-2471437b84bb1aef">Why predict expert error in addition to affinity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ace-guided-moe">Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Bar-Ilan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Affinity need not reflect expected next-token loss. An error head attenuates high-predicted-error logits before top-k and learns from actual next-token CE. Route using predictions available before the answer, not true CE.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Between similar experts, predicted error can promote the more suitable one without seeing the true next token online.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37751">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37751-ce-guided-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2471437b84bb1aef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ce-guided-moe" data-paper-title="Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ac282386e930a34f">How does error-aware routing differ from load balancing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ace-guided-moe">Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Bar-Ilan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Error-aware routing seeks token quality; balancing allocates compute evenly. Neither objective automatically supplies the other.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal token counts can still send difficult cases to unsuitable experts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37751">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37751-ce-guided-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ac282386e930a34f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ce-guided-moe" data-paper-title="Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-05e55b25b89a2afb">Is applying the error penalty after top-k equivalent?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ace-guided-moe">Cross-Entropy Guided Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Bar-Ilan University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Pre-softmax correction can change which experts are selected. Post-selection only reweights winners. Use true next-token CE to supervise the error head, not arbitrary heuristics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A third-ranked expert can replace a high-error first choice only before the selection is final.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37751">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37751-ce-guided-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-05e55b25b89a2afb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-cots-9dd74b8e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9f4fbec4454ef178">Why keep the sampled token rather than replace it with a soft token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Soft embeddings express alternatives but may drift from the sampled trajectory. The discrete anchor keeps at least half the weight while top-two competition controls the remainder.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Close candidates raise soft mixing without removing the sampled token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9f4fbec4454ef178">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-54d3e8b20e547876">How does CoTS preserve the sampled discrete trajectory under soft mixing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Top-two competition sets the mixing fraction, capped at half, so the sampled embedding remains at least half even outside the soft set. End-of-reasoning disables soft mixing permanently; format guards can affect one step.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Probabilities 0.6 and 0.4 give base mix 0.4 and keep 0.6 discrete; a larger gap weakens mixing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54d3e8b20e547876">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ecbeb97765865850">How does CoTS differ from averaging top-k embeddings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Form a probability-weighted soft vector and mix it with the discrete anchor using top-two-dependent α. An unweighted mean ignores probabilities and anchoring; phase-lock controls eligibility.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>0.9/0.1 and 0.5/0.5 distributions should not produce the same uniform representation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ecbeb97765865850">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:cots" data-paper-title="CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-70ae8db465d64ac8">Can soft mixing restart after the end-of-reasoning marker?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Acots">CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaomi AI Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Per-example phase-lock is irreversible starting at the step emitting &lt;/think&gt;. One-step format protection differs. Keep the discrete anchor even when it falls outside top-k.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Later close probabilities do not reopen mixing after a sample finishes reasoning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20642-cots/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-70ae8db465d64ac8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-elastic-expert-routing-bd240699" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-982dc49332289795">What is the fixed top-k exposure problem?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Experts just below rank k rarely receive the actual token computation and training. Elastic budgets give near-boundary experts chances before fixed-k deployment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>At k=2, a frequently third-ranked expert can be useful but rarely trained on those tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-982dc49332289795">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fd11a9699c42f50d">How does elastic routing preserve expected compute with a random expert count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A legal symmetric support centered at k balances more and fewer experts, keeping expectation k. Boundary experts get real sparse exposure. Deployment fixes k; training load counts actual dispatch, not fixed row length.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal probabilities for one, two, or three experts average two, but selecting three really costs more than one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fd11a9699c42f50d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0980348af90cb9c9">How does elastic budget perturbation differ from raising fixed k?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raising k always spends more. Symmetric perturbation preserves expected k while changing exposure. Match parameters, initialization, and average dispatch before comparing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal chances of two and four experts average three, not four every time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0980348af90cb9c9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:elastic-expert-routing" data-paper-title="Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2faf7156fa76811e">Why not truncate one side of the discrete Gaussian arbitrarily?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aelastic-expert-routing">Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai AI Laboratory / Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keep support symmetric around k and legal to preserve E[r]=k. Execute only selected experts, count actual loads, and fix k at inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Near the upper limit, deleting only the high side lowers mean budget.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.11575-elastic-expert-routing/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2faf7156fa76811e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-engram-7eeee5b9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0920b734f8751eb0">Why add lookup memory for frequent local patterns?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reconstructing common patterns repeatedly consumes compute. A learned n-gram table provides gated cached representations so attention and FFNs can focus on combinations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Look up a common phrase locally and compute novel combinations in the backbone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0920b734f8751eb0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-89a8dbb57f4df6dc">Why is Engram conditional memory rather than another set of MoE experts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MoE conditionally executes networks; Engram hashes normalized n-grams to deterministic table lookups and gates them into state. Stored patterns complement compositional compute, but memory size, collisions, bandwidth, and fusion cost remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A common phrase can fetch a vector, but context still determines its meaning here.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-89a8dbb57f4df6dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-40494fc31520acc4">How do Engram and MoE increase different resources?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MoE routes compute experts. Engram reads embeddings by n-gram address. O(1) lookup still requires storing, training, and moving table values.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Neural expert execution differs from fetching a phrase vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-40494fc31520acc4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:engram" data-paper-title="Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a110c6b00b2052be">Should Engram replace h_t with retrieved m_t?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aengram">Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · DeepSeek</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. h′=h+sigmoid(W[h;m])⊙m preserves the residual and gates by context. Record bucket count, n-gram orders, and added-parameter training budget; preserve small-budget negative results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A poorly trained memory should not overwrite the original hidden state unconditionally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a110c6b00b2052be">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lift-feedback" data-paper-title="Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-lift-feedback-608d6327" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a7da3ac89121a74">What carries deep information back to the next shallow step in LIFT?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alift-feedback">Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tel Aviv University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A continuous state accompanies the next discrete token. Training uses teacher top-k states and predicts token and next state; inference uses self-predicted states.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Pass a richer distribution alongside the generated word.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38149">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38149-lift-feedback/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a7da3ac89121a74">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lift-feedback" data-paper-title="Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c82cf42eda4038aa">Why predict next token and next continuous state in LIFT, and where does inference state come from?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alift-feedback">Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tel Aviv University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training turns the teacher&#x27;s top-k next-token distribution into a continuous input and jointly supervises token and state. This relays deeper signals beyond one token. Inference feeds back the model&#x27;s own state, not the teacher&#x27;s future distribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A sampled word can be accompanied by other likely alternatives in state; test accumulation of model feedback errors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38149">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38149-lift-feedback/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c82cf42eda4038aa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lift-feedback" data-paper-title="Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-98aacd6915e773b8">How does LIFT state feedback differ from returning only the sampled token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alift-feedback">Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tel Aviv University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A token preserves one discrete choice. State carries continuous top-k distribution information through the shared embedding space. Dedicated state supervision remains necessary; adding any extra vector is not equivalent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two nearly tied options contain information a single sampled word loses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38149">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38149-lift-feedback/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98aacd6915e773b8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lift-feedback" data-paper-title="Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec62d3d7947778b7">Can the student loss update LIFT teacher state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alift-feedback">Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tel Aviv University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Stop teacher gradients; train with token CE and forward KL on the normalized teacher top-k distribution. Inference must use the model&#x27;s own state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Student errors update the student, not teacher targets to match its mistakes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38149">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38149-lift-feedback/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec62d3d7947778b7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-lngram-v2-f7907f6f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-138ae0d1173848d4">Why turn hidden states into discrete n-gram addresses?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Recent-state combinations index a memory table in expected O(1); multiple results feed back into the backbone. Explicit addressing has a trainable projection and is not lookup of literal strings only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two binary hidden-state codes can form a 2-gram key.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-138ae0d1173848d4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-194361272e173289">Why use counterfactual neighbor addresses and a zero sink with hard Lngram v2 lookups?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Binary addresses are discrete and ordinary indexing gives no smooth address gradient. Neighbor comparisons train address choice. GQA reads retrieved tokens alongside a zero sink so irrelevant memory need not be injected.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A neighbor may be more useful than the addressed phrase; if neither helps, attend to zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-194361272e173289">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4e2fba325ae21ace">How do latent addresses differ from text n-gram hashes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Backbone hidden projections carry context, while text hashes depend directly on discrete input fragments. They do not share an address space or interpretation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same word in different contexts can yield different latent addresses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4e2fba325ae21ace">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:lngram-v2" data-paper-title="Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d7d21dd14de1dcdd">Why include a zero sink instead of always using lookup results?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alngram-v2">Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications / Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It lets GQA reject irrelevant memory. Counterfactual adjacent addresses supply training signals; the integer index is not ordinarily differentiable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A query can attend to zero to keep an unhelpful lookup out of the residual.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03426">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.03426-lngram-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d7d21dd14de1dcdd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:looped-latent-attention" data-paper-title="Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-looped-latent-attention-49effa17" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-48da7218fce331c6">How does sharing weights differ from sharing runtime state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alooped-latent-attention">Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The repeated transform is the same, but KV depends on each loop&#x27;s hidden inputs. LLA shares a latent while rebuilding each loop&#x27;s K/V.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One machine processing different intermediate materials produces different outputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15456">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.15456-looped-latent-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-48da7218fce331c6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:looped-latent-attention" data-paper-title="Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e51c5322d385eee9">Why can loop KV be compressed even when looped Transformer weights are shared?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alooped-latent-attention">Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Loops with shared weights still generate different KV. LLA stores shared low-rank latents and reconstructs loop-specific KV. Rank and error bound savings, and reconstruction costs compute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four iterations can store a small latent plus four maps rather than four full KV copies, subject to reconstruction quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15456">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.15456-looped-latent-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e51c5322d385eee9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:looped-latent-attention" data-paper-title="Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd8116bd4b27072b">What differs between LLA KV compression and reducing parameter count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alooped-latent-attention">Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weight sharing reduces parameter storage. Latent compression reduces history cache and adds reconstruction. Their memory scales differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Cache keeps growing with generated length while model weights remain fixed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15456">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.15456-looped-latent-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd8116bd4b27072b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:looped-latent-attention" data-paper-title="Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0bed63c0b7395852">What must stay loop-specific when reconstructing KV?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Alooped-latent-attention">Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Maryland / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A shared projection produces z, then separate loop matrices U reconstruct K/V. One identical KV for all loops removes the defining difference. The small model is not a post-hoc codec or fused server kernel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use U¹ and U² on the same z to produce two K outputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15456">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.15456-looped-latent-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0bed63c0b7395852">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-macro-6eaa3033" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-be5da7502289a7b9">Why treat layer execution as a program?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Context-conditioned Markov routes support skip, repeat, and residual-add rather than one fixed order. Feedback updates routes and candidate decoding chooses programs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One input can skip a layer and repeat another.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-be5da7502289a7b9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9feb28422bcc1fc0">How does MACRO change input computation without changing weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A context-conditioned routing program can skip, repeat, or residual-add layers. Feedback updates route probabilities and search selects programs; the backbone is fixed. Use validation, not isolated test gold, for selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two prompts can execute different paths through identical layers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9feb28422bcc1fc0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a661f3ccf921f6ab">What does routing search change compared with fine-tuning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It changes how fixed layers execute, not internal parameters. Costs and generalization can differ, and a route is not a new trained backbone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Rearranging blocks differs from reshaping them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a661f3ccf921f6ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:macro" data-paper-title="MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-223e9229767279e9">Can MACRO greedily concatenate the highest-probability operation at each step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amacro">MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Not generally. Top-k Viterbi preserves Markov dependencies. Locally greedy choices can miss a better full program; the classification mini-suite is not the paper&#x27;s scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A likely repeat now can reduce the score of all later reachable paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.05872-macro/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-223e9229767279e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-memory-grafting-16992e0e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ff481455d1eea76b">What are the roles of grafting model and recipient?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The grafting model supplies offline intermediate phrase states; the recipient reads this frozen memory online without rerunning the teacher for each phrase.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Encode phrases once and look up values later.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ff481455d1eea76b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-bda5b2f934f9e644">Why pre-encode frequent phrases and fall back to hashed Engram?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An offline model encodes common n-grams into frozen memory; the recipient tries longest-suffix exact lookup. Trainable hash memory covers misses. Projection and contextual gating decide how to use the result, separating offline knowledge cost from online access.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A common trigram hits the bank while a rare combination falls back to hashing; either can be gated away.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bda5b2f934f9e644">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-32a57367afab0c29">How does grafted memory differ from Engram trained from scratch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A pretrained model encodes and freezes the exact bank; longest-suffix lookup precedes trainable hash fallback. Table size alone is not the difference, and local results do not beat equal-parameter Engram.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An absent exact phrase uses the explicit hash fallback, not a fabricated value.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-32a57367afab0c29">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-grafting" data-paper-title="Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-934c6a4993813078">Which phrase state is stored in the offline bank?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-grafting">Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University / Microsoft Research Asia</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freeze the final token&#x27;s hidden state at the specified intermediate grafting layer. The recipient uses separate projection, context gate, and short convolution. End-to-end bank retraining changes the method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Store token four&#x27;s state for a four-word phrase rather than arbitrarily averaging all four.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20948">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.20948-memory-grafting/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-934c6a4993813078">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
