<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Replace the FFN with experts and dispatch each token to one. This grows capacity without computing all expert branches, although routing and communication remain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four experts can be available while one runs per token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f3ee5dc08bd3f4dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:switch-transformer" data-paper-title="Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ef6fd08ba273212">Why does top-1 Switch still need load balancing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswitch-transformer">Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Brain</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Top-1 caps experts per token but may concentrate traffic, bottlenecking winners and starving other experts. The auxiliary term combines actual dispatch proportions and mean router probabilities. More parameters do not imply proportional throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One of eight experts receiving 90% of tokens can overload despite one FFN per token.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ef6fd08ba273212">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:switch-transformer" data-paper-title="Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d0d41032af3ea7f6">How does true top-1 dispatch differ from computing all outputs then one-hot masking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswitch-transformer">Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Brain</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse dispatch executes selected experts only. Dense masking can match outputs while paying every expert&#x27;s cost. Inspect actual execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Computing four experts and discarding three is not one-expert compute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d0d41032af3ea7f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:switch-transformer" data-paper-title="Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cc5971522b46bfce">What do f_i and mean p_i count in Switch&#x27;s load term?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswitch-transformer">Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Brain</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>f_i is actual dispatch frequency; mean p_i is average router probability. Preserve the chosen expert&#x27;s gate. Local code does not cover capacity overflow or cross-device all-to-all.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>High dispatch and probability may correlate but are separate statistics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cc5971522b46bfce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swrouter" data-paper-title="SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-swrouter-da0aa5dd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-97a1eddae9f5d256">Why contract multi-turn context before routing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswrouter">SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Adjacent semantic similarity can identify repetition or unnecessary history. Construct a budgeted window first, then route on that context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Consolidate repeated clarifications before deciding what model is needed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.11414-swrouter/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-97a1eddae9f5d256">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swrouter" data-paper-title="SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d67fa349937aa021">Why evaluate SWRouter context compression separately from model choice?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswrouter">SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It first contracts conversation windows by adjacent semantic similarity, then routes. Losing a constraint can make even a good model fail; full context also does not guarantee a good route. Separate measurements locate failures.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If turn two changes the budget and compression drops it, don&#x27;t blame the routed model alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式或操作. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.11414-swrouter/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d67fa349937aa021">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swrouter" data-paper-title="SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-bfef1e3901b6f05a">How does semantic contraction differ from keeping the last few turns?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswrouter">SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A recency window assumes newer is better; semantic contraction uses adjacent meaning to segment. Compare context quality separately from routing accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An older key turn need not be removed merely because it is old.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.11414-swrouter/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bfef1e3901b6f05a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swrouter" data-paper-title="SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a5fad5f833524ce">Is local profile-overlap routing the paper&#x27;s trained contrastive encoder?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswrouter">SWRouter: Similarity-Contractive Window Routing for Multi-Turn Large Language Model Conversations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It executes segmentation and profile-overlap routing without contrastive training. Test these as separate local components, not as paper-level learned performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Selecting from keyword overlap shows rule execution, not learned contrastive representations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.11414-swrouter/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a5fad5f833524ce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-telescopic-lm-c2ab9fe1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cafa935d4f4aefa8">Why support multiple depths in one Telescopic checkpoint?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Budgets and inputs can need different depths. Supervise prefixes and full depth so shallow execution is an explicit trained option.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Choose a shorter prefix rather than train one checkpoint per depth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cafa935d4f4aefa8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ede6a79b9ddd5bb5">Why train multiple depth prefixes instead of truncating a finished deep model?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Standard training supervises the full path, not necessarily viable intermediate exits. Telescopic trains sampled prefixes with next-token supervision plus a full-depth anchor. Evaluate shallow and deep capabilities separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Running eight versus 24 layers is supported only if the eight-layer exit was explicitly trained.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ede6a79b9ddd5bb5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-37256dd8e30f5391">How do sampled prefixes differ from training all depths every step?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sampled training gives prefix supervision to selected depths plus the full anchor; all depths cost more per step. Match compute rather than only parameter count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One three-layer exit is not equivalent in cost to every exit from one to 12.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37256dd8e30f5391">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:telescopic-lm" data-paper-title="Telescopic Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5ba76aef5a3a17ce">How check that random prefixes do not replace the full-depth anchor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atelescopic-lm">Telescopic Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Cambridge</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Verify full-depth loss and gradients on every specified step and record the sampled depth. Local diagnostics do not reproduce 20B-token pretraining.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Even when sampling a shallow exit, confirm full-depth parameters still receive their signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35769">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.35769-telescopic-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5ba76aef5a3a17ce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:wide" data-paper-title="WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-wide-0e0ca0da" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-39ba580071e42696">Why give different tokens different model widths?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awide">WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · EIT-NLP / LMU Munich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Static pruning uses one subnetwork for all inputs. WIDE routes attention head groups and FFN channels separately to allocate token-specific compute within layers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Simple positions can use few groups while complex evidence gets more.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28418">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.28418-wide/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-39ba580071e42696">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:wide" data-paper-title="WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/conditional-compute">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c2aef9a999c0cef5">How is WIDE more fine-grained than skipping layers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awide">WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · EIT-NLP / LMU Munich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It chooses attention-head and FFN-channel groups per token within a layer. Real savings require mask rearrangement, block skipping, and device kernels. Dense zero-masking alone pays full compute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An easy token may use fewer groups than a hard token, but only skipped execution improves latency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ff571c81019b4be9">How does per-token width routing differ from pruning half the channels permanently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awide">WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · EIT-NLP / LMU Munich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed pruning removes the same groups; dynamic routing selects different groups by token. Even equal average sparsity has different paths and scheduling costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two tokens can each use half the groups without using the same half.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Conditional computation: experts, elastic depth and width, and lookup memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b4305e91a53784e8">How should WIDE masks interact with kernels to save work?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Awide">WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · EIT-NLP / LMU Munich</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Coordinate mask rearrangement, block skip, and on-device skipping. Multiplying a dense output by a mask does not remove matrix multiplication. Local PyTorch results are routing/sparsity/quality checks, not CUDA speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A zero head output does not prove its QK product was skipped.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<details class="ar-learning-guide" markdown="1"><summary>Topic guide and reading order</summary>

## Start with this question

At a fixed parameter budget, which parameters and how many steps should each token activate?

## Takeaway

Switch Transformer routes each token to a single expert and uses a balancing loss to avoid overloading a few experts. Engram adds learned n-gram hash lookup memory so computation need not reconstruct common patterns repeatedly. Dynamic depth, width, and recurrent steps further control compute by input. All separate total capacity from per-input activation cost.

## Example

One expert per token out of eight increases parameter count without eight FFNs per token, but popular experts can still queue. Hash lookup for common phrases trades compute for indexing and bandwidth. Neither form of sparsity removes communication, addressing, or parameter residency costs.

## Common pitfall

More experts do not imply proportionally more throughput. Imbalance, capacity overflow, and all-to-all communication can dominate. Lookups trade off collisions and capacity; repeated layers increase latency. Random routing diagnostics or registry labels are not capability or Evolve evidence.

## Reading order

Read Switch's top-1 routing and balancing first, then Engram's deterministic lookup and gated fusion. Distinguish conditional computation from memory, then choose depth, width, recurrence, or routing papers for the bottleneck.

1. [Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity](../../../../reproductions/2101.03961-switch-transformer/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)
2. [Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models](../../../../reproductions/2601.07372-engram/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372)

## Check your understanding

If an 80B MoE activates 8B parameters per token, does it only need to store 8B?

??? note "Show suggested answer"

    No. Active parameters describe current computation. All routable experts still have to reside somewhere or be loaded. GPU memory, communication, and FLOPs per step are different budgets. Report total and active parameters and measured cost.
